title: Dry spell sends Bengaluru's temperatures soaring, maximum at KIA up 5.7°C - Deccan Herald
full_text:
Bengaluru: A prolonged dry spell has pushed temperatures 3-4°C above normal across Karnataka, with Bengaluru likely to record maximum temperatures of around 33°C over the next five days, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) said.
The maximum temperature at Kempegowda International Airport (KIA) was 33.9°C, 5.7°C above normal. Bengaluru City recorded 32.6°C, or 4°C above normal, while HAL Airport recorded 32.1°C, 3.4°C above normal, according to the IMD’s daily weather report on Sunday morning.
However, temperatures eased later in the day. At 5.30 pm, Bengaluru recorded 30.2°C, just 1.6°C above normal, while HAL Airport recorded 30.4°C, 1.8°C above normal. The KIA figure was not immediately available.
IMD scientist CS Patil attributed the rise to a sharp decline in rainfall over the past one to two weeks, reduced soil moisture and fewer clouds. With limited cloud cover, more sunlight reaches the land surface, leading to faster daytime warming.
Patil said the conditions do not qualify as a heatwave, with no heatwave conditions currently prevailing. The absence of significant weather systems over the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea has also contributed to the dry spell. Without low-pressure systems or favourable wind circulation, moisture movement towards interior Karnataka remains limited.
Rainfall activity is expected to increase across Karnataka between September 13 and 14, though Bengaluru and other South Interior Karnataka districts may receive only scattered showers.
More rainfall could occur over south interior Karnataka after October 16, including Bengaluru, Kolar, Chikkaballapur, Ramanagara, Mandya, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, Kodagu, Hassan and Tumakuru, Patil said.
Karnataka has recorded a rainfall deficit of around 26% so far this year, compared with largely normal rainfall last year.
Patil advised farmers to consider less water-intensive crops, as inadequate rainfall could increase cultivation costs and crop losses. Any decision to declare additional areas drought-hit would be based on assessments of soil moisture, the duration of the dry spell and crop conditions.
